{{short description|American mathematician}}
'''Jane Margaret Hawkins''' is an American mathematician known for her research in  [[dynamical systems]] and [[complex dynamics]], including [[cellular automaton|cellular automata]] and [[Julia set]]s. She is a professor of mathematics at the [[University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill]].<ref name="unc">[http://janehawkins.web.unc.edu/ Jane M. Hawkins]; J. Hawkins, [http://janehawkins.web.unc.edu/home/other-publications/ How I became a mathematician].</ref> More recent research has included work on cellular automata models for the spread of [[HIV]], [[Hepatitis C]] and [[Ebola]].<ref>J. Hawkins and D. Molinek, Markov cellular automata models for chronic disease progression, ''International Journal of Biomathematics'', 8 (2015).</ref>

==Education and career==
Hawkins was raised in [[Schenectady, New York]]. Her father was a [[chemical engineer]].<ref name="unc" /> She graduated from the [[College of the Holy Cross]] in [[Worcester, Massachusetts]], with a [[Bachelor of Science]] in mathematics in 1976 as class valedictorian. She then won a [[Marshall Scholarship]] to pursue graduate studies in England, earning her [[M.S.|M.Sc.]] in mathematics and [[Ph.D.]] in mathematics specializing in [[catastrophe theory]] from the [[University of Warwick]] in 1981. Her doctoral dissertation, completed under [[Klaus Schmidt (mathematician)|Klaus Schmidt]], was titled, ''Type III Diffeomorphisms of Manifolds.''<ref>{{MathGenealogy|id=25005|title=Jane Hawkins}}; J. Hawkins, Dynamics of mathematical groups, in ''I, Mathematician'', ed. P. Casazza, S.G. Krantz and R.D. Ruden (Mathematical Association of America, 2015), 192-202.</ref>

She taught at the [[State University of New York, Stony Brook]] from 1980 to 1987, before moving to the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill.<ref>{{citation|url=https://appropriations.house.gov/sites/republicans.appropriations.house.gov/files/migrated/UploadedFiles/03.22.12_CJS_-_Members_and_Outside_Witnesses_-_Jane_Hawkins_-_Biography.pdf|title=Brief vita|year=2012|publisher=US Congress}}; {{citation|url=https://janehawkins.web.unc.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/17111/2019/01/hawkins-essay.pdf|title=Dynamics of mathematical groups|first=Jane M.|last=Hawkins}}</ref> Her book ''Ergodic Dynamics'' was published by Springer in 2021.<ref>{{cite book | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Yd0XEAAAQBAJ&q=hawkins+ergodic+dynamics | title=Ergodic Dynamics: From Basic Theory to Applications | isbn=9783030592424 | last1=Hawkins | first1=Jane | date=28 January 2021 | publisher=Springer }}</ref> Her book ''The Mathematics of Cellular Automata'' was published by AMS in 2024.<ref>{{cite book | url=https://bookstore.ams.org/view?ProductCode=STML/108 | title=The Mathematics of Cellular Automata | isbn=9781470475376 | last1=Hawkins | first1=Jane | date=23 Mar 2024 | publisher=American Mathematical Society }}</ref> And her third book, ''Mathematics for Artificial Intelligence'', was published in 2026.<ref>{{cite book | url=https://www.routledge.com/Mathematics-for-Artificial-Intelligence/Hawkins/p/book/9781041161974 | title=Mathematics for Artificial Intelligence | isbn=9781041161974 | last1=Hawkins | first1=Jane | date=19 Mar 2026 | publisher=Chapman & Hall }}</ref>

==Service==
In 2004, Hawkins presented testimony to a subcommittee of the [[United States House Committee on Appropriations|House Committee on Appropriations]] in support of grants to mathematical research, and again in 2012.<ref>[https://www.ams.org/policy/government/outreach/HawkinsTestimony.03-22-12.pdf Hawkins Testimony 3/22/12 ]</ref><ref>[https://www.ams.org/notices/200406/inside.pdf Hawkins presents testimony], ''Notices of the American Mathematical Society'' 51 (2004), 668.</ref> She served as Treasurer of the American Mathematical Society, chair of the AMS Investment Committee, and Board of Trustees Member from 2011 until February 1, 2021.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.ams.org/about-us/governance/officers/past-officers#treas|title = Past Officers and Executive Directors}}</ref> She is also a former AMS Council member at large.<ref>{{Cite web |title=AMS Committees |url=http://www.ams.org/about-us/governance/committees/mal-past.html |access-date=2023-03-27 |website=American Mathematical Society |language=en |archive-date=2023-03-06 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230306081906/https://www.ams.org/about-us/governance/committees/mal-past.html |url-status=dead }}</ref> Hawkins has done a lot of outreach for women in mathematics, most notably participating in the George Washington University's Summer Program for Women in Math (SPWM) as a faculty member, guest lecturer, and panel moderator between 1999 and its final year in 2013.<ref>[https://www2.gwu.edu/~spwm/  George Washington University SPWM]</ref>

==Recognition==
Hawkins was the first female valedictorian at the College of the Holy Cross.<ref>[https://www.holycross.edu/175th-anniversary/holy-cross-milestones Holy Cross Milestones]</ref>  In 2012, Hawkins became an inaugural fellow of the [[American Mathematical Society]].<ref>[https://www.ams.org/profession/fellows-list List of Fellows of the American Mathematical Society]</ref>

==Personal==
Hawkins is married to mathematician [[Michael E. Taylor]], whom she credits with encouraging her with continuing in research.<ref name="unc"/>
